result:
The kettle clicks off at precisely the right temperature, though I've never actually tested it with a thermometer, only with the particular hiss and shudder of water that has decided it is done being cold. I pour it into a mug that is slightly too large for the amount of tea I actually drink, which means I will have a small ring of amber left at the bottom after I've finished, a little lake no one will ever drink from. I watch the steam rise and curl into the kitchen air where it has nothing to hold it and so it simply disperses, becoming nothing, becoming the room again.

There is a strange comfort in the small rituals of a morning that no one else sees. The way I set the spoon against the saucer at a particular angle. The way I open the window because the air outside is thinner and colder and carries a faint smell of wet grass and the exhaust from a car three houses down. The way I step outside in just my socks and feel the tile floor bite into my feet, and I think, yes, this is a Tuesday, and I am alone in this house, and the world is doing its enormous indifferent turning while I stand here getting my toes cold.

I think often about how language is a kind of weather. It moves over the landscape of a life and changes what grows there. A single word, misplaced in a conversation twenty years ago, can alter the entire season of a friendship. A sentence overheard in a hallway when you were nine years old can follow you into every room you ever enter afterward, a small invisible animal that sleeps in the corner and wakes at 3 a.m. to look at you with red eyes. I remember my father saying, *You don't have to be the best at everything, you just have to be better than you were yesterday.* He said it gently, the way you'd tell a dog it was fine to stop fetching the ball. I was thirteen. I had just lost a chess match to a boy who chewed his nails. I thought he was being kind. I think now he was being kind, and also not quite meaning it, and that both things are true at once, and that that is the whole architecture of most love.

Outside the window, a woman is walking a grey dog that is walking itself, really, dragging her along by the leash like a small polite horse. She is looking at her phone. The dog has stopped to investigate a stain on the pavement with the focused intensity of a scientist examining a culture dish. She tugs the leash. The dog does not care. The dog has found the truth in that stain and is not leaving. I smile at this. The woman glances up, sees me looking, and offers a small apologetic nod, as if the dog's disobedience is her failure, as if she has not explained the rules clearly enough, as if the grey creature might, with the right tone of voice, simply *decide* to move on.

I go back inside. I make toast. I spread butter on it in a spiral, starting from the outside and working inward, because I have always done it this way and I cannot say why, and I press my thumb into the corner of the bread and it indents, a small soft crater, and I eat the toast standing at the counter because I cannot bring myself to sit down yet, because sitting down means the morning is officially started and the started morning means the other things, the emails, the phone calls, the small negotiations with the day about what will be acceptable and what will not.

There is a bird on the wire above the neighbor's roof. A sparrow, I think, though it could be a starling, though it is too small and too plain for that. It tilts its head. It tilts its head again. It is watching me, or the window, or the particular patch of sky behind me, and I feel the full ridiculous weight of being watched by a creature whose entire emotional life fits inside a walnut. It is not afraid of me. I am not afraid of it. We are two small warm things on opposite sides of a pane of glass, both of us slightly confused about why we are here, both of us going about our morning, and this is enough. This is, in fact, the whole point. Not to understand. Just to be here, warm, slightly confused, spreading butter in a spiral.

The toast gets cold. I eat it standing up. I wash the plate and dry it with a towel that smells faintly of lemon and iron, and I hang it on the rack where the other towels are, the one with the little frayed edge that I have been meaning to repair for six months, and I do not repair it, I never repair it, and the fraying gets longer by degrees so small I cannot see them happening, like my patience, like the afternoons, like the slow quiet subtraction of years from the ledger of my life.

I sit down now. I open the laptop. The screen glows a pale blue-white in the grey morning light and I stare at the cursor blinking in an empty document and I think, I could write anything, I could write about the sparrow, about the grey dog, about the stain on the pavement, about the way the steam from the kettle became the room, and I could write about my father and the chess match and the way a gentle sentence can be both true and insufficient, the way all true sentences are insufficient, the way a language made of finite words can only ever approximate the infinite wet particularity of a lived morning.

The cursor blinks. The cursor blinks. The cursor blinks.

And I type, and I stop, and I start again. And the day goes on.
